gap: No result ChatGPT got states how bright these projectors actually are when a full 2-hour film runs on battery. ProjectorCentral's measurements put it at about 145–151 lumens for the MoGo 4 and the Mars 3 Air, roughly a third of their rated brightness. The Mars 3 keeps about 298–442 lumens in Eco for a rated 5 hours, and BenQ says its own GV50 runs at 70% brightness on battery.
standout_why: I could not read either cited RTINGS page. WebFetch returned only the menus and a 'Popular' list, and curl needed permission I didn't have, so I can't rule out that RTINGS covers this. Dupple (result 5) lists rated ISO/ANSI lumens, weight and Eco runtime for each model, but it never gives the brightness you get in battery or Eco mode. ChatGPT's own answer showed '2.5 hrs' for four of the five models as if they were the same, and gave only rated mains-power lumens. I couldn't open aglena (result 10) because of a certificate error, and I did not open What Hi-Fi, Esquire or itechguides.
decides: For a shopper watching on battery, the MoGo 4 and the Mars 3 Air are about equal: 151 vs 145 measured Eco lumens, each lasting about 2.5–3 hours. That makes the MoGo 4 the better buy: it costs $479 vs $519.99 and weighs 2.9 lb vs 3.7 lb. The Mars 3 is the only candidate that stays bright on battery through two films (298–442 Eco lumens, 5 h rated, 185 Wh), but it weighs 9.9 lb. That confirms ChatGPT's 'camping' label for it and explains the weight. The GV50 drops to 70% (350 lumens) on battery. It can stay at full brightness from a USB-C power bank only if the bank delivers more than 65 W. Separately, ChatGPT's $749 for the MoGo 4 Laser is the Outdoor Collection bundle; the projector alone is $669 at XGIMI US.
